idiom_name: IDisposable + using statement/declaration (Dispose(bool) template, optional finalizer or SafeHandle)
implementation_notes: C# is the pattern's home: implement System.IDisposable, keep all cleanup logic in protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing), have the public non-virtual Dispose() call Dispose(true) followed by GC.SuppressFinalize(this), and cascade only to fields the type owns - the documentation states that a class which does not own an IDisposable field or property does not need to implement IDisposable at all. Callers collapse the protocol into a using statement or a using declaration, which the compiler rewrites into try/finally and which disposes multiple resources in reverse declaration order; release that must be awaited uses await using with IAsyncDisposable. Wrap raw OS handles in SafeHandle so the type rarely needs to write a finalizer itself.
pitfalls: Dispose(bool) must not touch other managed objects when disposing == false (the finalizer path): finalization order is unpredictable and those objects may already be gone.
Omitting GC.SuppressFinalize keeps finalizable instances alive for an extra collection and can run the cleanup path twice.
A using declaration covers the whole enclosing scope, so in a long method disposal happens much later than the logical end of use; a using statement scopes it exactly.

variants.name: IAsyncDisposable + await using (asynchronous teardown)
variants.implementation_notes: When release itself is asynchronous - flushing a network stream, sending a protocol goodbye, awaiting a rollback - implement IAsyncDisposable (optionally alongside IDisposable) and let callers write await using. The structure mirrors Dispose(bool): a public parameterless DisposeAsync() plus a protected virtual ValueTask DisposeAsyncCore() carrying the awaited cleanup, with the same idempotence and owned-only cascade rules. A finalizer cannot await, so any finalizable path keeps only the synchronous subset; plan for DisposeAsync to own everything that must be awaited.
pitfalls: A type implementing both IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable must keep the two paths consistent; mixing them (disposing synchronously on the async path) can deadlock or double-release.
DisposeAsyncCore must set the disposed flag before awaiting, otherwise a concurrent second call starts a second teardown while the first is still in flight.

await using requires the C# 8 compiler and a runtime with IAsyncDisposable, and the disposal is awaited only when the enclosing method is itself async and the scope exits normally or with an exception.
